rv.q: ...two-and-a-half hour stage send-off to their beloved horror anthology is a twisted joy
Stage/Fright, while exploring grief and ghosts, loses a little of that power. But it is so raucously entertaining that it fails to matter.
Stage/Fright takes the soggy old notion of the TV spin-off and invests it with love, care, surprises and skill.
Another wildly clever, madly innovative and suddenly moving show from this inspired duo.

So are Shearsmith and Steve Pemberton now winding down? Not a bit, if Stage/Fright is any guide. From its murderous prologue on – hands-down the most memorable mobile phone announcement ever made in a theatre – this live show is as twisty and unpredictable as the best of their episodes on the BBC.

Expect everything you love from the shows here: accents, slapstick, wigs, false teeth. It’s old-school laughs that still do the trick. As one of the younger members of the crowd, I suspect a good few references went over my head.
...an evening that gives the audience a good laugh – and a valuable fright
The show has a distinct feeling of using up the comedians' off-cuts, out-takes and left-overs for the amusement of themselves and their fervid fan-base.
The stage show is less high-voltage, partly because it has not mastered the telly's zooming closeups, both naturalistic and startling.
Fans will enjoy unpicking its snarl of tangled entrails
It's decent fun, directed with knockabout energy and great timing by Simon Evans.
It's surprising to find inspiration running so low in Steve Pemberton and Reece Shearsmith's things-that-go-bump-in-the-night spin-off.
It's not radical, or even as ground-breaking as the television shows which have spawned it. But it is great, all-encompassing fun.

Shearsmith and Pemberton are on fine form charging it with sparky wattage, fully flexing their elastic range by embracing the kitschy costumes, set changes, and slapstick dynamics of comedy double acts.
Diehard fans are sure to be satisfied
Still inventive and fun but short on sharp shocks

cn.t: Shearsmith and Pemberton's stage spin-off entertains with playful meta-theatricality, but critics find it struggles to sustain its TV formula across a full-length format, lacking the tight control and chills of the beloved series.
